clue.text: See 9
Mattress up on rock, poor thing?

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a mattress is a bed
a tor is a rocky peak

explanation.surface: A mattress is propped up on a rock, a sorry state for whoever owns it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: someone in debt is poor in the money sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who owes money is, broadly, short of funds and so a poor creature in financial terms.

clue.text: Olympian has dropped American underwear, plain lot in black and white

definitions.text: plain lot in black and white

indicators.note: something dropped is let fall away, so those letters leave the god's name

blocks.note: Zeus is the chief of the Olympian gods
US is the abbreviation for American
bras are items of underwear

explanation.surface: An Olympic athlete has abandoned American underwear while some people on the plain dress in monochrome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Olympian' suggests a modern athlete; here it is a god of Mount Olympus. 'Plain' is the grassland, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Zebras are striped animals living in herds on the African savanna, a striped group of grassland grazers.

clue.text: One's drunk at a formal occasion, so totally sozzled having quaffed last of tequila

definitions.text: One's drunk at a formal occasion

indicators.note: someone sozzled is very drunk and all over the place, so these letters lose their order
to quaff is to swallow, so the drunk letters take another inside them
the final letter of the word that follows is the only one kept

blocks.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
the drink's final letter

explanation.surface: A guest at a formal dinner gets thoroughly drunk after downing tequila.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' in the definition is the past participle of drink, describing the toast, not the guest.
explanation.definitionFit: The loyal toast is the toast to the monarch drunk at British formal dinners, so it is something drunk on such occasions.

clue.text: Playing field's to one side

blocks.note: a rec is short for recreation ground, a public playing field
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sports pitch is said to lie off to one side.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a rec is the local recreation ground or park with pitches.
explanation.definitionFit: Recto is the right-hand page of an open book, or the front of a leaf, as opposed to verso.

clue.text: See 18
Case of cryptic penned by syndicate of Guardian crossword setters arising

indicators.note: a case is the outside, so only the outermost letters of the next word are kept
something penned by another is enclosed by it, as in a pen

blocks.note: first and last letters of the word
from Paul's own point of view, the Guardian setters are our ring, a ring being a syndicate

explanation.surface: A cryptic case is written by a group of Guardian setters, rising up.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter speaks as one of the Guardian team, so their syndicate is 'our ring'.
explanation.definitionFit: Things arising are coming about or happening, which is what occurring means.

clue.text: Country lady wiping brow

indicators.note: the brow is the top, so in a down clue the topmost letter is wiped away

blocks.note: a lady is a woman

explanation.surface: A woman from the countryside mops her forehead.
explanation.definitionFit: Oman is a sultanate on the south-eastern Arabian peninsula, a nation state.

clue.text: Tennis tactic where ingenious prods desirable

indicators.note: ingenious suggests something cleverly reworked, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged
hot is slang for desirable

explanation.surface: A tennis plan is described where clever jabs are the thing to have.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop shot is a softly struck ball that barely clears the net, a deliberate ploy in tennis play.

clue.text: Put it another way, agent needs free share

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and can be rearranged

blocks.note: a rep, a representative, is an agent
letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sales agent asks for a share at no cost.
explanation.definitionFit: To express something in different words is to say it again in another form, which is the verb's sense.

clue.text: Wonderful vision, what might temporarily blind an officer?

definitions.text: what might temporarily blind an officer?

blocks.note: first meaning: a dialect phrase for a strikingly excellent or attractive person or thing

blocks.clueFragment: what might temporarily blind an officer?
blocks.note: second, playful meaning: a British police officer, so something dazzling one would blind him briefly

explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the phrase literally: a bobby is everyday British slang for a police officer, and a dazzler is anything that dazzles.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern English expression describes someone or something remarkably impressive or good-looking, a sight worth seeing.

clue.text: Reportedly something through which little dog jumps, experiencing such fun?

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so go by the sound of the phrase

blocks.clueFragment: something through which little dog jumps
blocks.note: a cocker spaniel is a small dog, and a performing dog leaps through a hoop; in non-rhotic British speech cocker ends like the a

explanation.surface: A circus act in which a small dog jumps through a hoop, great fun for all.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers a loose definition: a dog having such fun would be delighted.
explanation.definitionFit: Being cock-a-hoop means being jubilant and exultant, the state of someone having a great time.

clue.text: Searching on the ground floor as unlawful?

indicators.note: the tail of the last word is the signal: something awful is a mess, so the letters before it are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters up to the point where the last word splits, leaving its tail as the signal

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether searching the ground floor might be illegal.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is to split the final word as unl + awful; the question mark warns of that liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hunting on the ground is crawling on hands and knees, the posture the phrase describes.

clue.text: Emperor is some leader as tyrannical, in retrospect

indicators.note: some means only part of the words that follow, a run of letters inside them
looking back means the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: letters spanning the end of the first word, the second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: An emperor is judged in hindsight to be a somewhat tyrannical leader.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsar was the emperor of Russia before 1917.

clue.text: So unable to answer with some certainty

definitions.note: a whimsical reason rather than a synonym: you cannot answer when nothing was asked

blocks.note: first meaning, played for laughs: a reply is impossible when nothing has been asked
second meaning: an emphatic phrase saying something is beyond doubt

explanation.surface: A candidate is stumped and cannot reply, though sure of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening reads as being stumped by a hard question; the real reason is that there is nothing to answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying there is no question about something means it is beyond doubt, certainly so.

clue.text: Issue dipping into onion soup that's suspicious — good to eat?

indicators.note: something suspicious is fishy and not right, so these letters are rearranged
something dipping into another goes inside it

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged
a son is issue, offspring

explanation.surface: A child dips into a bowl of onion soup that looks dodgy and wonders whether it is safe to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: food that will not poison you is fit to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is free of toxins can be safely eaten, so it is fine as a meal.

clue.text: Frying liquid, reverberating sound around fan, I say!

indicators.note: around means the first part is wrapped about the next

blocks.note: a peal of bells or thunder reverberates
a nut is an enthusiast, as in fitness nut
oi is a call for attention

explanation.surface: A loud echoing noise surrounds a fan, prompting someone to shout.
explanation.definitionFit: Groundnut oil is a common cooking oil used for deep-frying.

clue.text: Dash marked with initial of engraver

indicators.note: an initial is the first letter, so only the opening letter of the next word is kept

blocks.note: stamped means marked, as with a seal
the word's opening letter

explanation.surface: An engraver's initial makes a mark on a dash of metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash' looks like the punctuation mark that would suit an engraver; it means a rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden headlong rush of a crowd or herd, a mad dash.

clue.text: Document in hand, left

blocks.note: to hand something over is to pass it
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A traveller has a document in hand and has departed.
explanation.definitionFit: A passport is the official paper that identifies a traveller and permits international travel.

clue.text: What's Gabon without love? It's totally unacceptable!

blocks.note: surface reading: a quiz question about the African country
setter's reading: take the O (love) out of the country's name and the four letters left are a familiar word jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone indignantly asks what a country would be without love, then condemns the very idea.
explanation.walkthrough: GABON minus O leaves GABN, which is BANG with its letters out of order, so the answer to the question is the exclamation itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom, meaning completely out of line, is an outraged verdict that something is beyond what can be tolerated.

clue.text: Bird has knocked figure on horse over

indicators.note: knocked over, with the next word, means toppled, so in a down clue the letters are turned bottom to top
over completes knocked over: something toppled ends up upside down

blocks.note: ten is a number, a figure
a nag is a horse

explanation.surface: A bird has knocked down a statue of a rider on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'figure on horse' puts the number above the horse before the whole is turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: The gannet is a large white seabird known for diving into the sea for fish.

clue.text: Tired and old battered Guardian employee?

indicators.note: something battered is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A worn-out, ageing newspaper staffer is a figure of self-deprecating fun.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: one editor among many people a newspaper employs.
explanation.definitionFit: An editor is a journalist who runs or checks content on a newspaper such as the Guardian.

clue.text: See 28
Reigning cats and dogs back in pluvial part of Australia

indicators.note: to dog is to follow closely, so the joining word comes after the next piece
the back of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: queens are female cats, punning on reigning queens
the word's last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: It is raining cats and dogs in a wet region of Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface borrows 'raining cats and dogs'; 'Reigning cats' are queens, and 'dogs' means follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Queensland is the north-eastern state of Australia.

clue.text: Classic location with English rider on order

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a rider is something added, like a postscript
the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: An English jockey is placed in order at a famous race venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rider' suggests a jockey; it is an addendum. The Classics are Britain's five great flat horse races, two of which are run at Epsom.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs racecourse in Surrey hosts the Derby and the Oaks, both Classic races.

clue.text: Roman god, King Christian, say

blocks.note: dio is Italian, the language of Rome, for god
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A list of religious figures: a god of Rome, a king, a Christian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a believer to go with the god and king; it is the first name of a couturier.
explanation.definitionFit: Christian Dior was the French fashion designer, so his surname is an example of someone called Christian.

clue.text: A smile and a wink, say, from crooked economist

definitions.text: A smile and a wink, say

indicators.note: something crooked is bent out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dishonest economist flashes a grin and a wink.
explanation.definitionFit: Emoticons are keyboard faces such as :-) and ;-), which stand for a grin and a wink, two examples.

clue.text: Cool fool, don't ya agree?

blocks.note: in means fashionable, cool
a nit, short for nitwit, is a fool

explanation.surface: A teenager calls someone a cool fool and seeks agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Innit is British slang contracting isn't it, a tag used to invite agreement.

clue.text: Cuckoo learnt to peck end off chocolate digestive

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so these letters go haywire and are rearranged
the end taken off a word is its last letter, the only one kept
to peck is to take a small bite, so the jumbled letters take another inside

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged
the word's final letter

explanation.surface: A cuckoo has learnt to nibble a chocolate biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chocolate digestive' is a British biscuit; here 'digestive' alone is the definition, an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Enteral means relating to the intestines, the gut, so it belongs to the digestive tract.

clue.text: Period remains connected with battle for a frightening number from the '6os

indicators.note: connected with says the battle is joined on to the other pieces, here at the front

blocks.note: Mons in Belgium was the site of a First World War battle
a term is a period, as of school or office
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: A historian links a stretch of time and some relics to a famous battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'connected with' tells you the battle joins the other pieces; the battle comes first in the answer even though it is clued last.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1962 novelty hit by Bobby Pickett is a horror-themed dance song, so a spooky musical number of that decade.
